A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LiteASR. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and references support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2 adds Appendix A, which is fully readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original transcription accuracy, encoder compression, hardware latency, kernel performance, and sensitivity experiments in Sections 2 and 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds quantization, calibration selection, repeated-seed, noise robustness, and compression sensitivity results in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The activation PCA, low-rank linear transformations, rank-selection constraints, and optimized self-attention procedure remain unchanged. Appendix A evaluates quantization compatibility without introducing a new LiteASR component.

E1.justification: The ESB, French/German MLS, and Japanese JSUT coverage is retained. Appendix A.3 adds a distinct corrupted-input scenario using Gaussian noise on LibriSpeech test.clean. The calibration studies reuse existing datasets, including MLS and JSUT as calibration sources.

E2.justification: Table 4 newly evaluates FasterWhisper INT8 quantization on original Whisper large-v3 and LiteASR configuration (b), alongside FP16 references. Existing main-text comparators remain unchanged. Newly cited pruning and low-rank speech methods are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The original Section 4 setup is retained, but Appendix A substantially extends the experimental protocols: FP16/INT8 comparisons, calibration counts of 10/100/200 and source-specific sampling, Gaussian noise with standard deviations from 0.01 to 0.1, and finer Turbo MLP thresholds between configurations (b) and (c). These are added experiments, not revisions of the original benchmark settings.

E4.justification: Appendix A adds substantial analyses of quantization compatibility, calibration quantity/domain/language/randomness, noise robustness, and the sharp Turbo accuracy decline between configurations (b) and (c). These supplement the retained layer-compression, threshold, language, and model sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions average latency over 10 runs. v2 additionally reports five independently seeded calibration/compression runs for large-v3 configuration (b): mean WER 10.15% with standard deviation 0.16 percentage points, and mean encoder size 378.5M with standard deviation 0.7M. It also clarifies that Table 1 reports a single instance.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the main speedup results are unchanged, while Tables 4–7 add substantial findings. Examples include balanced-model INT8 WER of 11.0 versus FP16 10.2, WER 11.4 with 10 calibration clips versus 10.2 with 100, and WER 56.2 for configuration (b) versus 46.7 for the original under noise standard deviation 0.1. Table 7 adds intermediate Turbo compression results. These are new experimental conditions, not improvements to retained same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Equations 1–16, the PCA derivation, rank constraints, attention identities, and computational-cost arguments are unchanged. The appendix introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical definition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and headline claims about encoder compression, reduced-dimensional attention, and accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Replacing expressions such as 'Pareto-optimal balance' with 'Pareto frontier' does not materially change their scientific scope.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds practical qualifications: diverse calibration data helps preserve accuracy, English calibration performs better in the reported tests, and stronger compression reduces severe-noise robustness. It also interprets Turbo's MLP sensitivity. These extend applicability guidance while retaining the central low-rank explanation and Section 7 limitations.

D1.justification: The appendix explicitly identifies English ESB as the original calibration source and documents source selection, FasterWhisper INT8 use, Gaussian noise injection into normalized audio, and SNR calculation for the added experiments. Existing code access, hardware, software versions, and calibration-time information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Winata et al. (2020) and Someki et al. (2025), distinguishes post-training activation compression from train-time low-rank architectures, and expands the discussion of resource requirements and complementarity with distillation and pruning. The overall research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language corrections, including 'perceptron' and 'character error rate,' standardizes dimensionality terminology, expands selected comparison passages, and adds Appendix A. The main section organization and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds appendix Tables 4–7 and reformats Figure 6 from one tall heatmap into two side-by-side blocks with shorter labels and a horizontal color scale. Its values are retained. Other displays remain essentially unchanged apart from minor captions and page reflow.

improvement.justification: The added calibration studies better support the 100-clip choice, quantify sensitivity to random selection, and reveal calibration-domain effects. Noise tests also expose a compression–robustness trade-off absent from v1. These improve validation and transparency, although seed statistics cover only one model/configuration and the principal benchmark evidence remains unchanged.
